verse.text: James, a slave of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion: greetings.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person who belongs to a master, and a first-century reader would have heard it that way. In the Greek Old Testament “slave of God” or “slave of the Lord” is also a title of honor for figures such as Moses and the prophets, so the word conveys both total belonging and dignity. Most English versions have “servant”; some have “slave” or “bondservant.”

“The Dispersion” was the established term for Jews living outside the land of Israel. Whether James is writing to Jewish followers of Jesus in particular, or uses “the twelve tribes” as a picture of the whole church, is debated.

verse.text: Consider it all joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you fall into trials of various kinds,
verse.note: The Greek plural was regularly used for a mixed group of men and women, and James is addressing whole congregations. Many recent translations render it this way; others keep “brothers.”

The word means a putting to the proof, and here it refers to hardships that test whether faith will hold. Older versions have “temptations,” which now suggests enticement to sin; most modern versions have “trials.” The same word returns in verse 12.

verse.text: knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance.
And let endurance have its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and whole, lacking in nothing.
verse.note: The Greek word means complete, fully grown, having reached its goal, and not flawless in the modern sense. Some versions have “mature” or “full effect” here. “Perfect” is kept because James repeats the word in verses 17 and 25, and the repetition appears deliberate.

verse.text: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given to him.
verse.note: The adverb’s basic sense is “simply, with singleness of purpose,” and in contexts of giving it shades into “generously.” It may instead mean “without reservation” or “without second thoughts,” which would set God’s single-minded giving against the double-minded asker of verse 8. Both readings have scholarly support.

verse.text: But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind.
verse.note: Standard lexicons give “doubt, waver” for this use of the verb, and almost all translations follow them. Some scholars argue that this sense is not clearly attested outside the New Testament in the period, and that the meaning is closer to “being divided” or “disputing,” that is, being at odds with oneself or with God. The image of the wave and the “double-minded” man in verse 8 fits either reading.

verse.text: For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord,
double-minded man that he is, unstable in all his ways.
Let the lowly brother boast in being raised up,
and the rich man in being brought low, because like a flower of the grass he will pass away.

note.term: like a flower of the grass

verse.note: The image and much of the wording of verses 10–11 come from Isaiah 40:6–8 in the Greek Old Testament, where all human glory is like a wildflower that withers while God’s word endures. It is disputed whether “the rich man” here is a fellow believer, with “brother” carried over from verse 9, or an outsider.

verse.text: For the sun rises with its scorching heat and dries up the grass, and its flower falls and the beauty of its appearance perishes. So too the rich man will fade away in the midst of his pursuits.
Blessed is the man who endures trial, because once he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have simply “he has promised,” with no subject stated. Later manuscripts add “the Lord” or “God.” “God” is supplied here only because English “he” would be confusing after “the man.”

verse.text: Let no one say when he is tempted, “I am being tempted by God,” for God cannot be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.
verse.note: The verb belongs to the same word-family as “trial” in verses 2 and 12, and its basic meaning is “put to the test.” James moves from outward hardships that test faith to the inward pull toward sin, as the references to evil, desire, and luring show, so “tempt” is used in verses 13–14. Some interpreters keep “test” throughout, reading the point as: no one under trial should blame God for it.

verse.text: But each person is tempted when he is dragged away and lured by his own desire.
Then desire, having conceived, gives birth to sin, and sin, when it is full-grown, brings forth death.
Do not be led astray, my beloved brothers and sisters.
Every good act of giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow cast by turning.
verse.note: “Lights” means the sun, moon, and stars, and God is called their Father as their creator. The words that follow use the language of astronomy: the heavenly bodies shift and cast changing shadows, but their maker does not change. The wording of the last phrase varies among the manuscripts and its exact sense is uncertain.

verse.text: Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, so that we would be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.
Know this, my beloved brothers and sisters. Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger,
verse.note: The Greek form can be a command (“Know this”) or a statement (“You know this”). Later manuscripts read a different word meaning “so then,” which is what older English versions translate.

verse.text: for a man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness of God.
Therefore, putting away all filth and overflowing wickedness, receive with gentleness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
verse.note: “Meekness” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a gentle, humble, unassertive disposition, here set against the anger of verses 19–20. “Gentleness” or “humility” is the usual modern rendering.

verse.text: But be doers of the word and not hearers only, deluding yourselves.
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks in a mirror at the face he was born with;
for he looks at himself and goes away, and at once forgets what he was like.
But the one who peers into the perfect law, the law of freedom, and stays with it, becoming not a hearer who forgets but a doer who acts—he will be blessed in his doing.
If anyone thinks he is religious while not bridling his tongue but deceiving his own heart, that person’s religion is worthless.
verse.note: The Greek words rendered “religious” and “religion” in verses 26–27 refer to the outward practice of worship—rites, observances, acts of devotion—and not to a system of beliefs. James’s point is that the worship God accepts consists in control of the tongue, care for the vulnerable, and moral integrity.

verse.text: Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to look after orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.
verse.note: The verb means to go to see someone out of concern for their welfare, and in the Greek Old Testament it is used of God coming to help his people. “Visit” now suggests a social call, whereas the point here is practical care for people in need. Most versions keep “visit”; some have “look after” or “care for.”

verse.text: My brothers and sisters, surely you do not hold faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ while showing favoritism?
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and James is writing to whole communities. “Brothers” alone now suggests to an English reader that only men are addressed. Where James means a single man or woman he says so, as in verse 15.

The Greek can be read either as a prohibition (“do not hold the faith … with favoritism”) or as a question expecting the answer “no.” Most English versions choose the command. The Greek edition translated here punctuates the sentence as a question, and this translation follows it. The practical force is much the same either way.

note.term: faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ
note.traditional: the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory

verse.note: The Greek is literally “the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory.” Most interpreters understand “faith of” as faith directed toward Jesus, but some take it as the faith or faithfulness that Jesus himself showed. The words “of glory” are also awkward: they may describe Jesus as glorious, name him “the Lord of glory,” or stand alongside his name as a title, “the Glory.”

verse.text: For if a man with gold rings and fine clothes comes into your assembly, and a poor man in filthy clothes also comes in,
verse.note: The Greek word is the one elsewhere rendered “synagogue.” It meant a gathering or the place where one was held. James uses it here for the meeting of Jesus’ followers, which suggests a community still at home in Jewish vocabulary.

verse.text: and you look with favor on the one wearing the fine clothes and say, “You sit here in a good place,” and to the poor man you say, “You stand, or sit down there by my footstool,”
have you not made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil reasoning?
verse.note: The verb can also mean “to be divided” or “to waver,” as it does in 1:6. On that reading James asks, “Are you not divided within yourselves?”, meaning torn between faith and the world’s standards. Either sense fits the context, and James may intend both.

verse.text: Listen, my dear brothers and sisters. Has God not chosen those who are poor in the eyes of the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom that he promised to those who love him?
But you have dishonored the poor man. Is it not the rich who oppress you, and they who drag you into the courts?
Is it not they who blaspheme the good name that was invoked over you?

note.term: the good name that was invoked over you
note.traditional: that worthy name by which you are called

verse.note: To have a name “called over” someone is an idiom from the Greek Old Testament marking that person as the property of the one named, as Israel belonged to God. Most interpreters take the name here to be that of Jesus, perhaps spoken over believers at baptism.

verse.text: If, however, you are carrying out the royal law in line with the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well.
But if you show favoritism, you are committing sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.
For whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at one point has become guilty of all of it.
For the one who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” Now if you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.
So speak and so act as people who are going to be judged by a law of freedom.
For judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if someone says they have faith but does not have works? Can that faith save them?
If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacks daily food,
verse.note: The Greek word covers both complete nakedness and being inadequately dressed, for example wearing only an undergarment or rags. The reply “keep warm” in the next verse shows that lack of adequate clothing is the point. Several modern versions translate similarly.

verse.text: and one of you says to them, “Go in peace; keep warm and eat your fill,” but you do not give them what the body needs, what good is it?
So too faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.
But someone will say, “You have faith and I have works.” Show me your faith apart from works, and I will show you my faith by my works.

note.term: You have faith and I have works

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had no quotation marks, and it is disputed where the imagined speaker’s words end and who “you” and “I” are. Since James himself champions works, the objector is hard to place. This translation follows the common view that the objector means “one person has faith, another has works,” as if the two could be separated, and that James replies from “Show me” onward. Others extend the quotation further or treat the speaker as an ally of James.

verse.text: You believe that God is one? You do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder.
verse.note: This is the central confession of Judaism, drawn from Deuteronomy 6:4 and recited daily. James grants that the belief is correct. His point is that correct belief alone is something even demons share.

verse.text: Do you want to be shown, you senseless person, that faith apart from works does not work?

note.traditional: is useless / is barren (KJV: is dead)

verse.note: The Greek adjective means “idle, not working, unproductive,” and it echoes the word for “works” in the same clause. “Does not work” keeps the pun, where the usual “useless” loses it. Some manuscripts read “dead” here, as in verses 17 and 26, which is the source of the King James wording. “Idle” is widely judged to be the earlier reading.

verse.text: Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered his son Isaac on the altar?
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two, so “justified” here and “righteousness” in verse 23 share a root. The verb can mean “declare to be in the right” or “show to be in the right, vindicate.” Many interpreters hold that James uses it in the second sense, of Abraham’s faith being proved genuine by what he did, and so does not contradict Paul’s statement that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. Others see a real difference of emphasis between the two writers.

verse.text: You see that faith was working together with his works, and by the works faith was made perfect,
verse.note: The verb means to bring something to its goal or finished state, not to remove flaws. James’s point is that Abraham’s faith reached its full, intended form in what he did. Some versions translate “was completed” or “was brought to completion.”

verse.text: and the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called a friend of God.
You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.
In the same way, was not Rahab the prostitute also justified by works when she welcomed the messengers and sent them out by a different road?
For just as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead.
Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers and sisters, knowing that we will receive a stricter judgment.
For we all stumble in many ways. If anyone does not stumble in speech, that person is perfect, able to bridle the whole body as well.
Now if we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we steer their whole body as well.
verse.note: Some manuscripts read “Look” (the reading behind the King James “Behold”) instead of “Now if.” The two Greek expressions were pronounced alike in the period and were easily confused by copyists. The text follows the reading printed in SBLGNT and most modern editions.

verse.text: Look at ships as well: though they are so large and are driven by harsh winds, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the impulse of the helmsman wishes.
So too the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. See how small a fire kindles how great a forest!
And the tongue is a fire. The tongue is set among our members as the world of unrighteousness; it stains the whole body, sets the wheel of existence ablaze, and is itself set ablaze by Gehenna.
verse.note: The grammar and punctuation of this sentence are disputed. The phrase can be attached to what precedes (“the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness”) or, as here, taken as what the tongue represents among the parts of the body: the unrighteous world in miniature. Either way the tongue is pictured as the place where the world’s wrongdoing is concentrated in a person.

note.traditional: the course of nature; the whole course of life

verse.note: The Greek is literally “the wheel of origin” or “of becoming.” Similar expressions were used in Greek religious and philosophical circles for the cycle of birth and death, but most scholars think that by this time the phrase had become a general expression for the whole round of human life. The image of the wheel is kept rather than paraphrased; the exact nuance is uncertain.

Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which had become the standard Jewish image for the place of final judgment. Many translations render it “hell,” usually with a footnote; the name is kept here so that it is not merged with Hades or with later imagery. This is the only occurrence of the word in the New Testament outside the Gospels.

verse.text: For every kind of wild animal and bird, of reptile and sea creature, is being tamed and has been tamed by humankind,
but the tongue no human being can tame—a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who have been made in the likeness of God.
From the same mouth come blessing and curse. My brothers and sisters, these things ought not to be so.
Does a spring gush sweet and bitter water from the same opening?
Can a fig tree, my brothers and sisters, produce olives, or a grapevine figs? Nor can salt water produce sweet.
Who among you is wise and understanding? Let that person show, by a good way of life, works done in the gentleness of wisdom.
verse.note: The traditional “meekness” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a humble, unassertive manner, here set against the jealousy and ambition of the next verse. “Gentleness” or “humility” is the usual rendering in modern translations.

verse.text: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, do not boast and lie against the truth.
verse.note: This word is rare outside the New Testament. Older translations linked it with a similar-sounding word for strife, but its few earlier occurrences concern self-seeking pursuit of position, and most modern scholars and translations render it “selfish ambition” or “rivalry.” The precise sense remains somewhat uncertain.

verse.text: This is not the wisdom that comes down from above; it is earthly, unspiritual, demonic.
verse.note: The adjective comes from the word for “soul” or “life” and describes what belongs to ordinary human life as opposed to what comes from God’s Spirit. The older rendering “sensual” wrongly suggests bodily appetites, and “natural” can sound like praise. Paul and Jude use the word in the same contrast with “spiritual.”

verse.text: For where there is jealousy and selfish ambition, there is unrest and every worthless practice.
But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peaceable, considerate, willing to yield, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, without hypocrisy.
verse.note: The word can mean either “not making distinctions,” that is, impartial, or “not divided,” that is, unwavering. James uses the related verb in both senses, for wavering in 1:6 and for discriminating between people in 2:4. Either meaning fits here, and scholars are divided.

verse.text: And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
verse.note: The Greek can equally mean “for those who make peace,” making the peacemakers the ones who benefit from the harvest rather than the ones who sow. Translations are divided between the two. “Fruit of righteousness” is likewise open to two readings: the fruit that consists in righteousness, or the fruit that righteousness produces.

Greek has a single word family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice,” and the verb traditionally rendered “justify.” The righteousness here belongs to the same family as the verb “justified” in 2:21–25. It means being in the right and doing what is right.

verse.text: Where do the wars and where do the fights among you come from? Is it not from this—from your pleasures, which are at war in the members of your body?

note.term: in the members of your body

verse.note: The Greek says simply “in your members,” meaning limbs or body parts. Most interpreters take this as the individual’s body, pictured as a battlefield of competing cravings. A minority take “members” as the members of the community, among whom the pleasures wage war.

verse.text: You desire, and you do not have; you murder and envy, and you cannot obtain; you fight and wage war. You do not have because you do not ask.

note.traditional: You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel.

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, and the clauses can be divided in more than one way. The translation follows the punctuation of the SBLGNT, which gives three parallel statements; many English versions instead divide so that murder is the result of frustrated desire and fighting the result of frustrated envy. Whether “murder” is literal or a deliberately shocking exaggeration is disputed.

verse.text: You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.
Adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? So whoever chooses to be a friend of the world becomes an enemy of God.
verse.note: The Greek word is feminine plural, “adulteresses.” It draws on the prophets’ picture of Israel as God’s unfaithful wife, so the charge is disloyalty to God, not sexual sin. Most modern versions paraphrase as “adulterous people”; later manuscripts expanded it to “adulterers and adulteresses,” which the King James Version follows.

verse.text: Or do you think that the Scripture speaks to no purpose when it says, “He longs jealously for the spirit he made to dwell in us”?
verse.note: No passage in the Hebrew Bible or its Greek translation matches the words that follow. They may summarize the scriptural theme of God’s jealousy for his people, quote a writing now lost, or—as some hold—the sentence may be a general statement about Scripture, with the actual quotation coming only in verse 6.

note.term: He longs jealously for the spirit he made to dwell in us
note.traditional: He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us

verse.note: This is one of the most disputed sentences in the letter. The Greek can also be read, “The spirit he made to dwell in us longs enviously,” describing the human tendency to envy; in favor of that reading, the word rendered “jealously” normally means envy, a vice not otherwise ascribed to God. The translation follows the majority of modern versions, which take God as the subject, in keeping with the image of unfaithfulness in verse 4. Some manuscripts read “the spirit that dwells in us.”

verse.text: But he gives greater grace. That is why it says, “God opposes the proud, but to the humble he gives grace.”

note.term: “God opposes the proud, but to the humble he gives grace.”

verse.note: The quotation is Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form, with “God” in place of “the Lord.” The same text is quoted in 1 Peter 5:5. The introductory words can be read as “it says” (Scripture) or “he says” (God).

verse.text: So submit to God. But resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into gloom.
Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will lift you up.

Do not speak against one another, brothers and sisters. Whoever speaks against a brother or sister, or judges a brother or sister, speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge.
verse.note: The Greek plural, traditionally “brothers” or “brethren,” was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women. James is speaking to the whole community, so the translation uses “brothers and sisters,” and “a brother or sister” for the singular later in the verse.

verse.text: There is one lawgiver and judge—the one who is able to save and to destroy. But you—who are you to judge your neighbor?
Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will travel to such-and-such a city and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”—
you who do not know what tomorrow holds—what your life will be! For you are a mist that appears for a little while and then disappears.

note.term: what tomorrow holds—what your life will be
note.traditional: you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life?

verse.note: The Greek is compressed, and the manuscripts differ slightly in wording. It can be read as one statement (“you do not know what your life will be like tomorrow”) or as a statement followed by a question (“What is your life?”). The sense is little affected.

verse.text: Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.”
But as it is, you boast in your pretensions. All such boasting is evil.
So for anyone who knows the good they ought to do and does not do it, for that person it is sin.
Come now, you rich people: weep and wail over the miseries that are coming upon you.
Your wealth has rotted, and your clothes have become moth-eaten.
Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasure in the last days.

note.traditional: will eat your flesh like fire

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, and “like fire” can go with what precedes or what follows. The SBLGNT edition punctuates it with the next clause, giving roughly “It is fire, as it were, that you have stored up in the last days.” This translation follows the reading of most English versions and commentators.

verse.text: Look! The wages of the workers who mowed your fields, the wages you held back, are crying out, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts.

note.traditional: Lord of hosts / Lord of Sabaoth / Lord Almighty

verse.note: James keeps the Hebrew word Sabaoth (“armies”) untranslated in his Greek, as the Greek version of Isaiah regularly does. The title pictures God as commander of the heavenly armies. The phrasing echoes Isaiah 5:9, where the same title appears in a denunciation of wealthy landowners.

verse.text: You have lived on the earth in luxury and self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter.
verse.note: The image is of animals that go on feeding on the very day they are to be butchered. The phrase recalls Jeremiah 12:3 and points to the day of God’s judgment, which the rich are approaching without knowing it.

verse.text: You have condemned, you have murdered the righteous one. Does he not oppose you?
verse.note: Most English versions read this as a statement about the defenseless victim: “he does not resist you.” The SBLGNT punctuates it as a question expecting the answer yes, and this translation follows that. On that reading “he” may be the murdered righteous one, now an accuser, or God, who “opposes the proud” (the same verb, in 4:6). “The righteous one” is most likely generic for the innocent poor, though some see a reference to Jesus.

verse.text: Be patient, then, brothers and sisters, until the coming of the Lord. Look: the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, patient over it until it receives the early and the late rains.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and James is writing to whole communities. “Brothers” alone would now suggest that only men are addressed. Several recent versions make the same choice; others keep “brothers” with a footnote.
The Greek word means arrival and presence. It was the regular term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city. Early Christians used it for the expected arrival of Jesus as Lord and judge.

verse.text: You too, be patient. Strengthen your hearts, because the coming of the Lord has drawn near.
Do not grumble against one another, brothers and sisters, so that you may not be judged. Look, the judge is standing at the doors.
Brothers and sisters, take as an example of suffering hardship and of patience the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.
Look, we call blessed those who endured. You have heard of the endurance of Job, and you have seen the outcome the Lord brought about: the Lord is full of compassion and merciful.
verse.note: The familiar phrase “the patience of Job” comes from the King James Version. The Greek word means holding out under pressure, not calm waiting, and Job in the biblical book is anything but calm. James uses a different word for “patience” in verses 7–10; “endurance” keeps the two apart and matches “those who endured” earlier in the verse. Most modern versions likewise use “endurance,” “steadfastness” or “perseverance.”

note.term: the outcome the Lord brought about
note.traditional: the end of the Lord / the purpose of the Lord

verse.note: Literally “the end of the Lord.” Most interpreters take this as the happy ending God gave to Job’s story (Job 42). Others take it as “the Lord’s purpose.” A few older interpreters saw a reference to the end of Jesus’ own life, which is now a minority view.

verse.text: But above all, my brothers and sisters, do not swear—not by heaven, not by earth, not by any other oath. Let your “Yes” be yes and your “No” be no, so that you do not fall under judgment.
Is anyone among you suffering hardship? Let them pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let them sing praise.
Is anyone among you sick? Let them call for the elders of the assembly, and let the elders pray over them, anointing them with oil in the name of the Lord.
verse.note: Nearly all English versions have “church,” and readers know what that refers to. To a first-century hearer the word meant a gathering of people: it was the term for a city’s civic assembly, and the Greek Scriptures use it for Israel assembled. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution, so this translation uses “assembly” throughout the New Testament.

verse.text: And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise them up; and if they have committed sins, they will be forgiven.

note.traditional: save the sick / make the sick person well

verse.note: The Greek verb covers both rescue from illness and salvation in the fuller sense, and “raise up” can likewise mean getting up from a sickbed or resurrection. Physical recovery is the primary sense in context, and some versions translate “make well.” “Save” is kept because James goes straight on to speak of sins forgiven and may intend both.

verse.text: So confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be healed. The petition of a righteous person has great power as it works.

note.traditional: the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much

verse.note: The final Greek word is a participle meaning “working” or “being made to work,” and its force is disputed. It may describe the prayer as active and effective, as rendered here. It may mean “when it is put into effect,” that is, when it is actually prayed. Or it may mean “when it is made effective” by God. English versions vary accordingly.

verse.text: Elijah was a human being just like us, and he prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three years and six months.
Then he prayed again, and the sky gave rain and the land produced its fruit.
My brothers and sisters, if anyone among you strays from the truth and someone turns them back,
that person should know that whoever turns a sinner back from their straying path will save that sinner’s soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.
verse.note: The Greek says only “his soul,” which could be the soul of the sinner who is brought back or of the person who brings him back. Most interpreters take it as the sinner’s, and the translation makes that explicit. Whose sins are “covered” is similarly open. The phrase echoes Proverbs 10:12 and appears also in 1 Peter 4:8.
